      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Colon <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Rectal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt0">Colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer is cancer</span></span> that develops in the tissues of the <span class="qt0">colon or rectum</span>. Your <span class="qt0">colon and rectum</span> are part of your digestive system:</p><ul><li>Your colon is the first and longest part of your large intestine. It absorbs water and some nutrients from foods. It also changes the leftover waste products into stool (poop).</li><li>Your rectum is the lower part of your large intestine. It's where your body stores stool.</li></ul><p><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> that begins in the colon is called colon <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer, and cancer</span></span> that begins in the rectum is called rectal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer. Cancer</span></span> that affects either of these parts may also be called <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p>What causes <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt0">Colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> happens when there are changes in your genetic material (DNA). These changes are also called mutations or variants. Often, the genetic changes that lead to <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> happen during your lifetime and the exact cause is unknown. But certain genetic changes that raise your risk for <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> are inherited, meaning that you are born with them.</p><p>Besides genetics, other factors, including your lifestyle and the environment, can affect your risk of <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p>Who is more likely to develop <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>Anyone can get <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, but certain factors make you more likely to develop it:</p><ul><li>Being older; your risk of getting <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> increases as you age.</li><li>Having a personal or family history of <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Having a history of adenomas. Adenomas are <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> polyps (growths) that look abnormal under a microscope or are 1 centimeter or larger. Adenomas are not <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, but they can sometimes turn into <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> over time.</li><li>Having a genetic syndrome such as familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) or Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>).</li><li>Having chronic ulcerative colitis or Crohn disease for 8 years or more.</li><li>Having three or more alcoholic drinks per day.</li><li>Smoking cigarettes.</li><li>Being Black; Black people have an increased risk of <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> and death from <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> compared to other races.</li><li>Having obesity.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt0">Colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> may not always cause symptoms, especially at first. If you do have symptoms, they could include:</p><ul><li>A change in bowel habits that lasts more than a few days, such as:
	<ul><li>Diarrhea</li><li>Constipation</li><li>Feeling that the bowel does not empty completely</li><li>Your stool is narrower or has a different shape than usual</li></ul>
</li><li>Blood (either bright red or very dark) in the stool</li><li>Frequent gas pains, bloating, fullness, or cramps</li><li>Weight loss for no known reason</li><li>Fatigue</li></ul>What is screening for <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> and who needs it?<p>Because <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> may not cause symptoms at first, it's important to have screening tests for <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. Screening tests look for signs of a disease before you have any symptoms. They can help find <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> early, when it may be easier to treat.</p><p>Most experts recommend that start screenings at 45 and continue until at least age 75. People over 75 and those who are at high risk should talk to their providers about how often you need screening and what type of test they should get.</p><p> The types of tests include different stool tests and procedures such as colonoscopies and flexible sigmoidoscopy. Talk with your provider about how often you need screening and what type of test you should get.</p>How is <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>If you have symptoms that could be caused by <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> or if your screening test results are abnormal, you may need to have more tests to find out if you have <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. Possible tests include:</p><ul><li>A physical exam.</li><li>A digital rectal exam. For this exam, your provider inserts a lubricated, gloved finger into your rectum to feel for lumps or anything unusual.</li><li>The tests that are also used for screening (colonoscopy, stool tests, etc.) and biopsy, if you have not already had them.</li><li>Other blood and tissue tests.</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>Your treatment options usually depend on your age, your general health, how serious the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is, and which type of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> you have.</p><p>For colon <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, your treatment may include one or more of these options:</p><ul><li>Surgery.</li><li>Radiofrequency ablation, a procedure that uses radio waves to heat and destroy abnormal cells. The radio waves travel through electrodes (small devices that carry electricity).</li><li>Cryosurgery, a procedure in which an extremely cold liquid or an instrument called a cryoprobe is used to freeze and destroy abnormal tissue.</li><li>Chemotherapy.</li><li>Radiation therapy.</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that mainly attack specific <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells and cause less harm to normal cells.</li><li>Immunotherapy.</li></ul><p>For rectal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, your treatment may include one or more of these options:</p><ul><li>Surgery.</li><li>Radiation therapy.</li><li>Chemotherapy.</li><li>Active surveillance, which means having regular tests to see if your rectal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> has changed. If the tests show the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is starting to grow, then you will have treatment to try to cure the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that mainly attack specific <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells and cause less harm to normal cells.</li><li>Immunotherapy.</li></ul>Can <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>Avoiding the risk factors that you have control over may help prevent some <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>. That includes:</p><ul><li>Not smoking</li><li>Limiting alcohol to under three drinks per day</li><li>Managing your weight</li></ul><p>There are also other steps you can take to try to prevent <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. They include:</p><ul><li>Getting regular <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> screenings</li><li>Having polyps removed before they can become cancerous</li><li>Getting regular exercise</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/colonoscopy.html">
      <content name="title">Colonoscopy</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Sigmoidoscopy</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are colonoscopy and flexible sigmoidoscopy?<p>Colonoscopy and flexible sigmoidoscopy are procedures that let your doctor look inside your <span class="qt0">rectum and colon</span> (large intestine). They use instruments called scopes. Scopes have a light and a tiny camera attached to a long, thin tube. These procedures let your doctor see problems such as inflamed tissue, ulcers, polyps, and <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>Colonoscopy checks your entire <span class="qt0">colon and rectum</span>. Flexible sigmoidoscopy checks the rectum and the lower colon (sigmoid colon) only.</p>What is a virtual colonoscopy?<p>A virtual colonoscopy also looks inside your rectum and part of your colon. But it does not use a scope. Instead, it is an x-ray test. Another name for this test is CT colonography.</p>Who needs a colonoscopy, virtual colonoscopy, or flexible sigmoidoscopy?<p>You may need a colonoscopy, virtual colonoscopy, or flexible sigmoidoscopy to find the cause of unexplained symptoms such as:</p><ul><li>Bleeding from your anus (the opening of the rectum through which stool passes out of your body)</li><li>Changes in your bowel activity, such as diarrhea</li><li>Pain in your abdomen (belly)</li><li>Unexplained weight loss</li></ul><p>Doctors also use these procedures to screen for colon polyps and <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. Screening is testing for diseases when you have no symptoms. It may find diseases at an early stage, when they are easier to treat. If aren't at higher risk for <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, your health care provider will likely recommend you start getting screenings at age 45. If you are at higher risk, you may need to start getting screened for <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> earlier.</p><p>There are also other tests to screen for <span class="qt0">colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, including stool tests. Talk with your provider about which test is right for you and when and how often you should get it.</p>How do you prepare for a colonoscopy, virtual colonoscopy, or flexible sigmoidoscopy?<p>To prepare for a colonoscopy, virtual colonoscopy, or flexible sigmoidoscopy, you will need to:</p><ul><li>Talk with your doctor about any health problems you have and all of the medicines and supplements that you take. You may need to stop taking some of your medicines and/or supplements before the procedure.</li><li>Follow the bowel prep instructions from your doctor. The bowel prep clears the stool out of your colon, so your doctor will be able to see the colon during the procedure:
	<ul><li>You may need to follow a clear liquid diet, usually for about one day before the procedure. Avoid red or purple drinks or gelatin; the dye can look like blood in the colon. You probably need to stop eating and drinking the night before the exam.</li><li>You will need to take some laxatives. They may be pills, a powder that you dissolve in liquid, an enema, or a combination of these. The laxative will cause diarrhea, so you need to stay close to the bathroom.</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>For a virtual colonoscopy, you will also need to drink a contrast medium the night before. The contrast medium is a dye or other substance that is visible on x-rays. It can help your doctor tell the difference between stool and polyps.</p>How are colonoscopy, virtual colonoscopy, and flexible sigmoidoscopy done?<p>For a colonoscopy:</p><ul><li>You will have the procedure at a hospital or outpatient center. It usually takes 30 to 60 minutes.</li><li>You will get IV (intravenous) sedatives or anesthesia, usually along with pain medicine, so you won't be awake or feel pain during the procedure.</li><li>You'll lie on a table while the doctor inserts a colonoscope through your anus and into your <span class="qt0">rectum and colon</span>. The scope inflates your large intestine with air for a better view. The camera sends a video image to a monitor so your doctor can see your colon.</li><li>Once the scope reaches the opening to your small intestine, the doctor will slowly remove the scope. While doing so, your doctor will examine your colon again.</li><li>If you have polyps, your doctor may remove them and send them to a lab for testing. Most polyps aren't <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, but removing them can prevent them from becoming <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> later on.</li><li>If you have abnormal tissue, your doctor may do a biopsy.</li><li>The sedative or anesthesia takes time to wear off completely. You'll stay at the hospital or outpatient center for 1 to 2 hours after the procedure. Then you will need someone to drive you home.</li></ul><p>For a virtual colonoscopy:</p><ul><li>You will have the procedure at a hospital or outpatient center. It usually takes about 10 to 15 minutes.</li><li>You do not need anesthesia.</li><li>You'll lie on a table while a specially trained x-ray technician inserts a thin tube through your anus and into your rectum. The tube inflates your large intestine with air for a better view.</li><li>The table slides into a tunnel-shaped device where the technician takes the x-ray images. You will turn over on your side or stomach to get more images taken.</li></ul><p>For a flexible sigmoidoscopy:</p><ul><li>You will have the procedure at a hospital, medical office, or outpatient center. It usually takes about 20 minutes.</li><li>You do not need anesthesia.</li><li>You'll lie on a table while the doctor inserts a thin tube through your anus and into your rectum. The tube inflates your large intestine with air for a better view. The camera sends a video image to a monitor so your doctor can see your lower colon.</li><li>Once the scope has reached the top of the lower colon, the doctor will slowly remove the scope. While doing so, your doctor will examine your lower colon again.</li><li>If you have polyps, your doctor may remove them and send them to a lab for testing. Most polyps aren't <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, but removing them can prevent them from becoming <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> later on.</li><li>If you have abnormal tissue, your doctor may do a biopsy.</li></ul>What should I expect after a colonoscopy, virtual colonoscopy, or flexible sigmoidoscopy?<p>You may feel cramping in your abdomen or bloating during the first hour after the any of these procedures. If the doctor removed polyps or performed a biopsy, you may have light bleeding from your anus. This bleeding is normal.</p><p>For a virtual colonoscopy or a flexible sigmoidoscopy, you go back to your regular activities and diet right after the test. For a colonoscopy, you can expect a full recovery and return to your normal diet by the next day.</p><p>Your doctor will give you the results of your procedure. If you had a biopsy, it can take a few days to get those results.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="title">Colonic Polyps</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Colon polyps</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A polyp is an extra piece of tissue that grows inside your body. Colonic polyps grow in the large intestine, or colon.  Most polyps are not dangerous. However, some polyps may turn into <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> or already be <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. To be safe, doctors remove polyps and test them.  Polyps can be removed when a doctor examines the inside of the large intestine during a colonoscopy.</p><p>Anyone can get polyps, but certain people are more likely than others. You may have a greater chance of getting polyps if you :</p><ul><li>	Are over age 50 </li><li>	Have had polyps before </li><li>	Have a family member with polyps </li><li>	Have a family history of colon <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> </li></ul><p>Most colon polyps do not cause symptoms. If you have symptoms, they may include blood on your underwear or on toilet paper after a bowel movement, blood in your stool, or constipation or diarrhea lasting more than a week.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/healthscreening.html">
      <content name="title">Health Screening</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Screening Tests</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Screenings are tests that look for diseases before you have symptoms. Screening tests can find diseases early, when they're easier to treat. You can get some screenings in your doctor's office. Others need special equipment, so you may need to go to a different office or clinic.</p><p>Some conditions that doctors commonly screen for include:</p><ul><li>Breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> and cervical <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> in women</li><li><span class="qt0">Colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span></li><li>Diabetes</li><li>High blood pressure</li><li>High cholesterol</li><li>Osteoporosis</li><li>Overweight and obesity</li><li>Prostate <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> in men</li></ul><p>Which tests you need depends on your age, your sex, your family history, and whether you have risk factors for certain diseases.  After a screening test, ask when you will get the results and whom to talk to about them.</p><p>Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/colonicdiseases.html">
      <content name="title">Colonic Diseases</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Intestinal Diseases</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Large intestine diseases</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your colon, also known as the large intestine, is part of your digestive system. It's a long, hollow tube at the end of your digestive tract where your body makes and stores stool. Many disorders affect the colon's ability to work properly. Some of these include:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Colorectal</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span></li><li>Colonic polyps - extra tissue growing in the colon that can become cancerous</li><li>Ulcerative colitis - ulcers of the <span class="qt0">colon and rectum</span></li><li>Diverticulitis - inflammation or infection of pouches in the colon</li><li>Irritable bowel syndrome  -  an uncomfortable condition causing abdominal cramping and other symptoms</li></ul><p>Treatment for colonic diseases varies greatly depending on the disease and its severity. Treatment may involve diet, medicines and in some cases, surgery.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>
